citeinfo.title: Loch Vale Watershed hydroclimate and isotopes of tree-ring cellulose and source-water isotope model
Testing tree-ring cellulose d18O with water isotopes for Holocene lake d18O interpretations in the central Rocky Mountains USA
citeinfo.othercit: Anderson, L., Mast, A., Brice, B., Berkelhammer, M.B. (2025) Testing tree-ring cellulose d18O with water isotopes for Holocene lake d18O interpretations in the central Rocky Mountains USA. The Holocene 35(1):18-28.

descript.abstract: Stable isotopes of water preserved in geologic archives, primarily as oxygen (d18O), have proven critical for documenting Earth’s climatic and hydrologic systems past and present. However, timescale differences of water isotope inputs to proxy systems and the signal embedded in long paleorecords often confound translation to observed hydroclimatic metrics. Here, a unique 20-year dataset of meteorology, hydrology, and the isotopic composition of weekly meteoric and surface water samples (d18O, d2H) are combined with paleoclimate d18O data from tree-ring cellulose and lake carbonate to better understand proxy signals of Upper Colorado river basin drought. Annual tree-ring cellulose d18O from Picea engelmannii growing within a glacier-fed creek and a spring discharge area were used to derive annual source water d18O using a cellulose source-water isotope model. Comparisons with the monitoring record indicates that tree-ring cellulose d18O tracks variations in wet and dry hydroclimatic extremes. The data release contains the annual tree-cellulose isotope data with hydroclimate and water isotope annual averages, including those used for the cellulose source-water isotope model.
descript.purpose: The data were collected to better understand proxy signals of Upper Colorado River basin drought and is appropriate for use with related climate reconstruction techniques and scientific objectives.

procstep.procdesc:
The Andrews Creek and Loch Vale watershed environmental and water collections began in various years in the 1990s and by 1998 all the datasets are continuous through 2017. Weekly collections include Andrews Creek, the spring, and precipitation samples from a station located at Loch Vale (Scholl et al., 2023). Integrated snowpack in Andrews Meadow and adjacent forest was sampled near April 1 (Anderson et al., 2016b). Hydrologic and meteorological observations in the Andrews Creek and Loch Vale watershed include hourly temperature data from three stations at 2885m (Bear Lake SNOTEL; USDA NRCS, 2014), 3160 m (Loch Vale Main), and 3206 m (Loch Vale Andrews) (USGS NWIS, 2024). Bear Lake temperatures were corrected for sensor upgrade in 2005 (Mast and Ingersoll, 2011; Oyler et al., 2015). Weekly precipitation amounts are from Loch Vale. Andrews Creek discharge is measured daily.
Over the 20-yr period that water samples were collected and analyzed for stable oxygen and hydrogen isotopes, different laboratories and methods were used. Detailed information is available for each sample from the U.S. Geological Survey National Water Information Systems web interface (USGS NWIS, 2024) and is summarized here. Analytical methods include use of laser cavity ring-down analyzers at the U.S. Geological Survey Boulder National Research Program Laboratory (Los Gatos), the Colorado School of Mines Isotope Laboratory (Picarro), and the University of Utah SIRFER Laboratory (Picarro) by injecting 1microliter into a heated vaporization chamber and the vapor stream carried into the cavity of the laser absorption spectrometer. All samples were measured six times and the first three injections rejected due to the influence of carryover. Additional residual memory corrections are applied to the last three injections, which are then averaged to generate the reported value. Uncertainty is reported as the absolute range of the three injections and is <0.2‰ and <0.5‰ for oxygen and hydrogen, respectively. Secondary water isotope standards are run intermittently to assess drift and in-house span standards were analyzed at the end of each run to correct results to the VSMOW (Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water) scale. The methods closely follow those previously described by Gupta et al., (2009) and Brand et al., (2009). All mass spectrometry analyses were carried out at the USGS Reston Stable Isotope Laboratory by automated constant temperature equilibration with CO2 for oxygen and automated H/D preparation by chromium reduction. The 2-sigma uncertainty of 0.2‰ and 2‰ for oxygen and hydrogen, respectively, with normalization to Standard Light Antarctic Precipitation (SLAP) values of -428‰ and -55.5‰ for oxygen and hydrogen, respectively. All water results are reported in per mil (‰) as the relative difference of isotope ratios (d,delta) from the international measurement standard VSMOW defined by d18OH2O = ([18O/16O]H2O /[18O/16O]VSMOW) -1 and d2HH2O = ([2H/1H]H2O /[2H/1H]VSMOW) -1. Annual amount weighted precipitation values (calendar or water year) were calculated from annual isotope averages and precipitation amounts. To calculate weighted monthly values, weekly measurements were used to calculate monthly isotope averages weighted by monthly precipitation as an annual fraction. Within season precipitation amount weighting was found to have an insignificant effect on seasonal isotope averages.
Tree-ring sampling was conducted in September 2016 and targeted mature and healthy P. engelmannii growing in and immediately adjacent to Andrews Creek and within the spring discharge area. From a total of 9 trees, eighteen tree cores were obtained (2 cores per tree) using a large diameter borer (12 mm). To achieve a stand average, 5 cores were selected for isotope analyses based on wide well-defined annual rings of 50 to 80 years in length without regard to tree location. This resulted in 3 cores from Andrews Creek and 2 cores from the spring. Visual cross dating followed standard methods although statistical verification was not possible due to the short core lengths and small interannual ring width variation. For each of the 5 cores, whole annual rings for years from 1994 to 2015 were individually sampled by a razor blade for cellulose extraction by a Brendel extraction method modified for small sample sizes (Anchukaitis et al., 2008). Purified cellulose of ~2 microgram weight was packed in silver capsules and analyzed by TC-EA coupled with a mass spectrometer at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Results are reported in per mil (‰) as the relative difference of isotope ratios (d, delta) from the international measurement standard VSMOW defined by d18OCELL = ([18O/16O]CELL /[18O/16O]VSMOW) -1. Pure cellulose and in-house sucrose standards (n=40) regularly interspersed throughout the samples (n=115) indicated analytical uncertainty of ± 0.3‰.
